This theoretical diversity reflects the complexity of consciousness itself. Some theories primarily explain access, attention, and reportability. Others aim at phenomenal experience, embodiment, selfhood, or metaphysical foundations. The result is not one unified theory, but a pluralistic field with multiple competing and overlapping explanatory frameworks.

### Consciousness-First and T-Consciousness Frameworks

A further contemporary development involves consciousness-first frameworks, which treat consciousness not as a late product of biological or neural complexity, but as a more fundamental aspect of reality. These approaches differ from standard physicalist, functionalist, and neurobiological theories because they do not begin with matter, computation, or neural activity as the primary explanatory foundation.

Taheri’s T-Consciousness theory can be placed within this broader consciousness-first landscape. In this view, consciousness is not produced by the brain in the ordinary materialist sense. Rather, consciousness is treated as a non-material and foundational reality through which life, mind, and organization become manifested. This makes T-Consciousness different from theories that explain consciousness primarily through neural mechanisms, information processing, or biological evolution [@taheri2020; @taheri2023].

Historically, T-Consciousness is best understood as part of a recent expansion of consciousness studies beyond standard neuroscience and cognitive science. It shares some broad concerns with panpsychism, cosmopsychism, and other consciousness-first theories, but it also differs from them in its emphasis on non-material consciousness fields and the idea that life is revealed or manifested through consciousness rather than generated solely by material processes.

Because T-Consciousness is not yet part of the mainstream scientific consensus, it should be presented carefully as an emerging or alternative framework rather than as an established scientific theory. Its importance in the history of consciousness research lies in how it illustrates a wider contemporary movement: the attempt to reconsider whether consciousness may be foundational rather than derivative.

## Artificial Intelligence and Machine Consciousness

Artificial intelligence represents one of the newest phases in the history of consciousness research. As AI systems become more capable of language use, pattern recognition, planning, and adaptive behaviour, researchers increasingly ask whether such systems could ever be conscious.

The question is partly theoretical. If consciousness depends primarily on functional organization, information processing, or self-modeling, then artificial consciousness may be possible in principle. Functionalist and computational theories are often more open to this possibility [@putnam1967; @fodor1975; @dehaene2017].

However, biological and embodied approaches are more cautious. They argue that current AI systems may simulate intelligent behaviour without possessing subjective experience. From this perspective, consciousness may require bodily regulation, affect, homeostasis, biological needs, or active engagement with an environment [@varela1991; @thompson2007; @seth2021].

Machine consciousness also raises ethical questions. If an artificial system could become conscious, then issues of moral status, artificial suffering, autonomy, rights, and responsibility would become important. If artificial systems are not conscious, then there remains a risk of anthropomorphism: mistakenly attributing experience to systems that merely produce convincing outputs [@butlin2023].

AI therefore brings old questions into a new context. The mind-body problem becomes the mind-machine problem. The question of subjective experience becomes the question of whether computation can feel like anything from the inside.

## Contemporary Interdisciplinary Research

Modern consciousness studies is highly interdisciplinary. It draws from neuroscience, cognitive science, philosophy of mind, psychology, artificial intelligence, phenomenology, psychiatry, biology, physics, information theory, and complexity science.

This interdisciplinarity is not accidental. Consciousness appears to involve multiple explanatory levels. Neural mechanisms are important, but they do not by themselves settle questions about subjective experience. Computational models are useful, but they may not fully capture embodiment, affect, or lived experience. Phenomenology describes experience, but it must still be related to brain, body, and world. Philosophical analysis clarifies concepts, but it must remain connected to empirical findings.

Contemporary consciousness research therefore increasingly combines methods. Researchers compare theories through experiments, study altered states, investigate disorders of consciousness, model neural dynamics, analyze subjective reports, and examine artificial systems. The field remains open because no single approach has yet explained consciousness completely.

## Current State of the Field

The contemporary field remains theoretically pluralistic. There is no universally accepted theory of consciousness, no single agreed definition, and no consensus about whether consciousness can be fully reduced to physical, functional, computational, or informational processes.

This lack of consensus is sometimes seen as a weakness, but it may also reflect the complexity of the subject. Consciousness includes wakefulness, awareness, attention, selfhood, reportability, metacognition, embodiment, affect, and phenomenal experience. Different theories may explain different dimensions of this larger problem.

The history of consciousness research shows that progress often occurs through conceptual refinement as much as through empirical discovery. Behaviourism improved scientific rigor but marginalized experience. Cognitive science restored internal mental processes but often treated consciousness indirectly. Neuroscience made consciousness experimentally tractable but did not eliminate philosophical questions. AI introduced new questions about computation, agency, and moral status.

The field therefore remains scientifically productive and philosophically open-ended.

## Main Historical Conclusion

The historical development of consciousness research reveals an expanding attempt to understand one of the deepest problems in science and philosophy. The field has moved from metaphysical reflection to introspective psychology, from behaviourism to cognitive science, from neuroscience to artificial intelligence, and from single-discipline approaches to interdisciplinary theory.

This history does not show a simple path toward one final theory. Instead, it shows that consciousness repeatedly exceeds the boundaries of any single framework. Philosophical questions persist within neuroscience. First-person experience returns after behaviourist exclusion. Computation raises new versions of old mind-body problems. Embodiment challenges purely internal models of mind. Artificial intelligence forces renewed attention to the difference between intelligence and experience.

Modern consciousness science increasingly recognizes that consciousness may require explanation across neural, computational, phenomenological, embodied, biological, and philosophical levels. The field remains unsettled not because it has failed to progress, but because its central question is unusually deep: how does subjective experience fit into the natural world?

## Chapter Summary

The history of consciousness research shows how the field has changed across major intellectual periods. Classical and early modern philosophers framed consciousness through questions of soul, mind, matter, perception, and selfhood. Early psychologists attempted to study experience through introspection, while behaviourists later rejected consciousness as a scientific object and focused on observable behaviour.

The cognitive revolution reintroduced internal mental processes and information-processing models. Neuroscience then transformed consciousness into an empirical research program through the study of neural correlates, altered states, anesthesia, sleep, and disorders of consciousness.

Contemporary consciousness studies is now interdisciplinary. It includes theories based on global access, integrated information, higher-order representation, recurrent processing, prediction, attention modeling, embodiment, panpsychism, illusionism, and artificial intelligence.

The central historical lesson is that consciousness research has never been only one kind of inquiry. It is philosophical, psychological, neuroscientific, computational, phenomenological, biological, and ethical. Its history explains why the field remains pluralistic today.

<!--chapter:end:04-historical-development.Rmd-->

# Dualism {#dualism}

## Chapter Overview

Dualism is one of the oldest and most influential approaches in the philosophy of mind and consciousness studies. Broadly defined, dualism holds that consciousness cannot be fully reduced to physical processes alone. Mental states, subjective experience, and first-person awareness are treated as fundamentally distinct from, or at least not exhaustively explainable by, purely material descriptions of the brain.

Dualist theories arise largely from dissatisfaction with reductionist accounts of consciousness. Neuroscience may explain neural activity, perception, memory, cognition, behaviour, and decision-making with increasing precision. Yet dualists argue that such explanations may still leave something important unexplained: why conscious experience exists at all and why experience has qualitative, first-person character.

This concern connects dualism directly to the hard problem of consciousness. If physical descriptions explain brain mechanisms but do not explain why those mechanisms are accompanied by subjective experience, then consciousness may require a different kind of explanation [@chalmers1995; @chalmers1996]. Dualism is one of the major philosophical responses to this problem.

This chapter examines dualism as a family of positions rather than a single theory. It introduces the historical origins of dualist thought, distinguishes major forms of dualism, explains why dualism remains important in contemporary consciousness studies, and evaluates its strengths, limitations, and implications for neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and the study of subjective experience.

## Learning Objectives

After reading this chapter, the reader should be able to:

* Define dualism in the philosophy of mind.
* Distinguish substance dualism, property dualism, interactionism, epiphenomenalism, and naturalistic dualism.
* Explain the relationship between dualism and the hard problem of consciousness.
* Describe the explanatory gap that motivates many dualist arguments.
* Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of dualist explanations.
* Compare dualism with physicalist, functionalist, and computational theories.
* Assess the implications of dualism for neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and subjective experience.

## What Dualism Claims

Dualism begins from the idea that mind and matter cannot be understood as exactly the same kind of thing. Physical objects can be described in terms of mass, extension, location, motion, structure, and causal interaction. Conscious experience, by contrast, seems to involve subjectivity, feeling, intentionality, perspective, and qualitative awareness.

The central dualist claim is not simply that the brain and consciousness are different words. Rather, the claim is that physical description may not fully capture what consciousness is. A complete account of neural activity might describe electrical signals, neurotransmitters, brain networks, and behavioural outputs. But dualists argue that such an account may still fail to explain what it is like to undergo an experience.

This is why dualism remains important even in a scientific age. It challenges the assumption that explaining brain mechanisms automatically explains consciousness. Dualism asks whether subjective experience can be reduced to physical processes, or whether consciousness reveals something incomplete in purely material explanation.

## Historical Development

Questions about the relationship between mind and matter existed long before modern neuroscience. Ancient philosophical traditions debated the nature of soul, perception, selfhood, life, and awareness. However, dualism became especially influential in early modern philosophy through René Descartes.

Descartes argued that mind and body are fundamentally different kinds of substance. Matter is extended in space and governed by mechanical laws, whereas mind is characterized by thought, awareness, and subjectivity [@descartes1641]. This view became known as **substance dualism**.

Cartesian dualism strongly shaped the modern mind-body problem. If mind and body are different substances, then one must explain how they relate to one another. How can subjective thought interact with physical matter? How can conscious intention move the body? How can brain processes give rise to experience?

Although contemporary neuroscience rarely accepts Cartesian substance dualism in its original form, many contemporary debates still inherit dualist concerns. The hard problem, the explanatory gap, debates about qualia, and questions about first-person experience all reflect the continuing difficulty of explaining consciousness in purely physical terms [@nagel1974; @levine1983; @chalmers1996].

Twentieth-century behaviourism temporarily marginalized consciousness by focusing psychology on observable behaviour rather than private experience [@watson1913; @skinner1953]. Later, the cognitive revolution reintroduced internal mental processes into psychology, while neuroscience made consciousness increasingly available to empirical study. However, these developments did not eliminate dualist questions. Instead, they sharpened them: even if cognition and neural mechanisms can be studied scientifically, does this fully explain subjective experience?

## Dualism and the Hard Problem

Dualism is closely connected to the hard problem of consciousness. The hard problem asks why physical or computational processes are accompanied by subjective experience at all [@chalmers1995]. Dualism offers one possible answer: perhaps subjective experience cannot be fully explained because it is not reducible to physical processes in the first place.

This does not mean that all dualists reject neuroscience. Many contemporary dualists accept that the brain is deeply involved in consciousness. They may agree that changes in brain activity correspond to changes in experience. What they deny is that neural correlation alone provides a complete explanation of phenomenal consciousness.

The distinction between **access consciousness** and **phenomenal consciousness** is especially important here [@block1995]. Access consciousness concerns information that is available for reasoning, report, memory, and action. Phenomenal consciousness concerns qualitative experience itself: what it is like to see red, feel pain, hear music, or experience oneself as a subject.

Dualist theories are usually motivated by phenomenal consciousness. A physicalist or functionalist theory may explain how information becomes available for report and action. The dualist question is whether such an explanation also explains why there is something it is like to have the experience.

## Major Forms of Dualism

Dualism is not a single unified theory. It is a family of positions concerning the relation between consciousness and the physical world. These positions differ in how strongly they separate mind from matter and in how they understand the causal relationship between mental and physical states.

### Substance Dualism {#substance-dualism}

Substance dualism is the view that mind and matter are fundamentally different substances. On this view, the physical body belongs to the material world, while the conscious mind belongs to a non-physical domain. Descartes is the most famous defender of this position [@descartes1641].

Substance dualism has intuitive appeal because conscious experience seems very different from physical matter. Thoughts, feelings, and sensations do not appear to occupy space in the same way that physical objects do. However, substance dualism faces a serious challenge: if mind is non-physical, how does it interact with the physical brain and body?

This is known as the interaction problem, and it remains one of the strongest objections to Cartesian dualism.

### Property Dualism {#property-dualism}

Property dualism rejects the idea that mind and body are separate substances. Instead, it argues that conscious experience involves properties that are not reducible to physical properties. On this view, consciousness may arise from physical systems, but phenomenal experience cannot be fully explained in physical terms.

Property dualism is more compatible with contemporary science than traditional substance dualism. It does not require a separate mental substance. However, it still claims that physical descriptions leave out something essential about experience.

Chalmers’ naturalistic dualism is often understood as a form of property dualism. He argues that consciousness may be a fundamental feature of reality governed by psychophysical laws, rather than something reducible to known physical processes [@chalmers1996].

### Interactionist Dualism {#interactionism}

Interactionist dualism holds that mental and physical states can causally influence one another. Conscious intentions may affect bodily actions, while brain events may affect conscious experience. This view preserves the ordinary intuition that conscious decisions matter and that mental life plays a causal role in behaviour.

The difficulty is explaining how this interaction occurs. If physical events are fully governed by physical laws, then it is unclear how non-physical mental events could influence the brain without violating causal closure. This challenge has been central to critiques of dualist mental causation [@kim2005; @papineau2002].

### Epiphenomenalism {#epiphenomenalism}

Epiphenomenalism holds that physical brain processes produce conscious experience, but conscious experience does not itself cause physical events. On this view, consciousness is real but causally inert. It accompanies neural activity without influencing behaviour.

Epiphenomenalism avoids some versions of the interaction problem because it does not require consciousness to act back on the physical world. However, it creates other difficulties. If consciousness has no causal role, then it becomes difficult to explain why humans talk about consciousness, why conscious pain seems to guide action, or why experience would have evolved.

Frank Jackson’s original knowledge argument was often associated with epiphenomenalist intuitions, although Jackson later revised his position [@jackson1982].

### Naturalistic Dualism {#naturalistic-dualism}

Naturalistic dualism attempts to combine scientific realism with the claim that consciousness is fundamental. Chalmers argues that consciousness may require new basic principles linking physical processes with experience [@chalmers1996]. These would not be supernatural principles, but they would go beyond current physical explanation.

Naturalistic dualism is important because it does not reject science. Instead, it argues that science may need to expand its explanatory framework to include consciousness as a fundamental feature of reality.

This position is closely related to broader debates about whether consciousness can be reduced, whether it must be treated as fundamental, and whether a future science of consciousness may require psychophysical laws.

## Conceptual Framework

Dualism can be understood as a response to the explanatory gap between physical description and subjective experience. The gap arises because objective science describes mechanisms, structures, functions, and causal relations, while consciousness appears as first-person experience [@levine1983].

Figure @ref(fig:fig-dualism-gap) illustrates this tension.

```{r fig-dualism-gap, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Dualism and the explanatory gap. Dualist theories argue that subjective experience cannot be fully reduced to physical or cognitive explanation alone.", out.width="90%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/03_dualism_explanatory_gap.png")
```

As Figure @ref(fig:fig-dualism-gap) suggests, dualist theories do not usually deny that neural activity and cognitive processing are important. Rather, they argue that explanations at these levels may remain incomplete if they do not account for phenomenal experience itself.

Figure @ref(fig:fig-dualism-triangle) places dualism within the broader conceptual structure of consciousness studies.

```{r fig-dualism-triangle, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="The central explanatory domains involved in consciousness research. Dualist approaches emphasize the difficulty of fully reducing subjective experience to neural or computational accounts alone.", out.width="86%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/03_central_triangle.png")
```

As shown in Figure @ref(fig:fig-dualism-triangle), consciousness research involves at least three domains: neural mechanisms, cognitive or informational processing, and subjective experience. Dualism emphasizes the claim that subjective experience cannot be fully derived from the other two domains alone.

## Dualism and Qualia

Dualism is strongly motivated by the problem of **qualia**, the qualitative features of conscious experience. Qualia include the redness of red, the painfulness of pain, the taste of bitterness, the sound of music, or the feeling of warmth.

The problem is that qualia do not seem easily captured by objective description. A scientist may describe the wavelength of red light, the structure of the retina, the activation of visual cortex, and the behavioural ability to identify colours. Yet the dualist argues that this still may not explain what red looks like from the first-person point of view.

This concern is closely related to Nagel’s argument that subjective experience has a perspectival character that cannot be fully captured by objective science [@nagel1974]. It is also central to Jackson’s Mary’s Room thought experiment, where complete physical knowledge seems insufficient to provide knowledge of what colour experience is like [@jackson1982].

Dualism therefore forces the question: are qualia reducible to physical and functional descriptions, or do they reveal an irreducible aspect of consciousness?

## The Interaction Problem

The interaction problem is one of the most important objections to dualism. If consciousness is non-physical, how can it affect the physical brain? If conscious intention causes bodily movement, then mental events seem to influence physical events. But if the physical world is causally closed, then every physical event already has a sufficient physical cause [@papineau2002].

This creates a dilemma for dualism. If consciousness affects the physical world, dualism must explain how this interaction occurs. If consciousness does not affect the physical world, then dualism risks epiphenomenalism, where consciousness becomes causally irrelevant.

This problem is especially serious for substance dualism. Property dualism and naturalistic dualism sometimes attempt to avoid it by treating consciousness as dependent on physical systems while still irreducible. However, critics argue that the problem of mental causation remains unresolved [@kim2005].

## Mental Causation and Agency

Dualism is also connected to questions of free will, agency, and intentional action. In ordinary life, people experience themselves as making choices, forming intentions, and acting for reasons. Dualism often preserves the intuition that conscious decisions genuinely influence behaviour.

However, many physicalist theories argue that behaviour can be explained through brain processes without appealing to non-physical mental causation. From this perspective, conscious intention may be part of the physical causal order rather than something outside it.

The challenge is to explain how subjective agency fits with neuroscience. If all behaviour is physically caused, what causal role does conscious intention play? If consciousness has no causal role, why does agency feel so central to human life?

Dualism keeps these questions visible, even when it does not fully solve them.

## Empirical Relevance and Scientific Challenges

Dualism is primarily a philosophical position, but it has implications for empirical consciousness research. Studies of anesthesia, dreaming, blindsight, split-brain patients, disorders of consciousness, and altered states all raise questions about the relation between neural activity and conscious awareness [@laureys2005; @owen2006; @koch2016; @seth2018].

Dualists may interpret such cases as evidence that consciousness cannot be reduced simply to behaviour or report. For example, a patient may show limited behavioural responsiveness while still possibly retaining some form of awareness. A person with blindsight may respond to visual stimuli without ordinary conscious seeing. Split-brain cases raise questions about unity of consciousness and the relation between brain organization and subjective selfhood.

However, these cases do not automatically prove dualism. Physicalist, functionalist, and neuroscientific theories can also explain many of these phenomena. A major challenge for dualism is that it often lacks clear empirical tests that would distinguish it from non-dualist explanations.

This is one reason many scientists regard dualism as philosophically significant but scientifically difficult to operationalize.

## Strengths of Dualism

Dualism has several important strengths. First, it directly confronts subjective experience rather than reducing consciousness immediately to behaviour, computation, or neural function. It insists that a theory of consciousness must explain experience itself.

Second, dualism highlights the difference between first-person and third-person explanation. This distinction remains important even for researchers who reject dualism, because consciousness studies must still relate subjective reports to objective measurements.

Third, dualism provides a powerful critique of overly reductionist theories. It asks whether explanations of attention, memory, reportability, or information processing are sufficient to explain phenomenal consciousness.

Finally, dualism preserves the philosophical importance of qualia, selfhood, agency, and the apparent reality of inner life. Even if dualism is ultimately rejected, the problems it raises continue to shape contemporary theories.

## Weaknesses of Dualism

Dualism also faces major weaknesses. The most serious is the interaction problem. If consciousness is non-physical, it is difficult to explain how it affects the physical world. If it has no effect, then it becomes difficult to explain agency, decision-making, and the apparent causal role of experience.

Dualism also faces challenges of empirical testability. Many versions do not provide clear experimental predictions or measurable markers that would distinguish dualism from physicalist theories.

Another criticism is that dualism may explain mystery by adding more mystery. Instead of explaining how consciousness arises, it may simply declare consciousness irreducible. Critics argue that this can weaken dualism as a scientific theory.

Some philosophers also argue that dualism relies too heavily on intuition and thought experiments. Dennett, for example, argues that many traditional assumptions about qualia are misleading and that consciousness should be explained through cognitive functions and information-processing capacities [@dennett1991]. Illusionists go further by arguing that phenomenal consciousness, as traditionally conceived, may itself be a cognitive illusion [@frankish2016].

## Dualism and Artificial Intelligence

Dualism has important implications for artificial intelligence. If consciousness depends only on functional organization or information processing, then artificial consciousness may be possible in principle. But if consciousness involves non-reducible mental properties or fundamental phenomenal features, then computational sophistication alone may not be sufficient.

This creates a major contrast between dualist and functionalist approaches. Functionalism suggests that a system with the right causal organization could be conscious, regardless of whether it is biological or artificial [@putnam1967; @fodor1975]. Dualist approaches are more cautious. They ask whether artificial systems could possess subjective experience rather than merely simulate intelligent behaviour.

Recent debates about AI consciousness often turn on this distinction. A system may produce language, solve problems, model itself, and report internal states, yet it remains unclear whether there is anything it is like to be that system [@dehaene2017; @butlin2023].

Dualism therefore challenges the assumption that intelligence and consciousness are the same. It reminds us that behavioural sophistication does not automatically settle questions about subjective experience.

## Dualism and Other Theories

Dualism differs from physicalism, functionalism, and computationalism in its treatment of subjective experience. Physicalism argues that consciousness is ultimately physical. Functionalism argues that mental states are defined by their causal roles. Computationalism treats cognition, and sometimes consciousness, in terms of information processing.

Dualism accepts that these approaches may explain many aspects of mind. However, it denies that they necessarily explain phenomenal consciousness. From the dualist perspective, a theory that explains cognition has not automatically explained experience.

Dualism also differs from panpsychism, although both resist simple reductionism. Panpsychism argues that consciousness or proto-consciousness may be fundamental and widespread in nature [@goff2017]. Dualism, especially in its Cartesian form, more strongly separates mind and matter. Naturalistic dualism and panpsychism can sometimes overlap, but they are not identical.

This comparison shows why dualism remains useful even when one does not accept it fully. It clarifies what is at stake when theories claim to explain consciousness.

## Evaluation

Dualism remains one of the most historically influential and philosophically significant approaches to consciousness. Its central contribution is that it keeps subjective experience at the center of the discussion. It challenges any theory that explains cognition, behaviour, or neural activity while leaving phenomenal consciousness unexplained.

At the same time, dualism faces serious difficulties. Substance dualism struggles with the interaction problem. Property dualism must explain how irreducible mental properties fit into the physical world. Epiphenomenalism risks making consciousness causally irrelevant. Naturalistic dualism requires new explanatory principles that remain difficult to specify and test.

For this reason, dualism is often more powerful as a critique than as a complete scientific theory. It identifies a problem that physicalist and functionalist theories must address, but it does not always provide a clear mechanism or empirical research program of its own.

Whether dualism is ultimately correct remains deeply contested. Nevertheless, nearly every major theory of consciousness must respond to the questions dualism raises: Can subjective experience be reduced to physical processes? Is consciousness a physical, functional, or fundamental feature of reality? Does explaining the brain explain the mind? And can a complete science of consciousness avoid the first-person character of experience?

## Chapter Summary

Dualism is the view that consciousness cannot be fully reduced to physical processes alone. Its most famous historical form is Cartesian substance dualism, which treats mind and matter as distinct substances. Contemporary forms include property dualism, interactionism, epiphenomenalism, and naturalistic dualism.

Dualism is motivated by the hard problem of consciousness, the explanatory gap, and the difficulty of explaining qualia through objective physical description. It emphasizes phenomenal consciousness rather than access consciousness alone.

The strengths of dualism include its direct focus on subjective experience, its critique of reductionism, and its emphasis on the difference between first-person and third-person explanation. Its weaknesses include the interaction problem, limited empirical testability, difficulties concerning mental causation, and the risk of introducing additional metaphysical mystery.

Dualism remains important because it forces all theories of consciousness to confront the problem of subjective experience. Even theories that reject dualism must explain why consciousness seems difficult to reduce to brain mechanisms, computation, or behaviour alone.

<!--chapter:end:05-dualism.Rmd-->

# Physicalism and Materialist Theories of Consciousness {#physicalism}

## Chapter Overview

Physicalism is the view that everything that exists is ultimately physical in nature, including consciousness. According to physicalist approaches, conscious experience does not require a separate mental substance, immaterial soul, or fundamentally non-physical reality. Instead, consciousness is understood as depending on physical systems, neural organization, biological processes, computational dynamics, or information-processing structures.

Physicalism is the dominant working framework within contemporary neuroscience and much of cognitive science. This is because consciousness is closely connected to brain activity, bodily regulation, behaviour, perception, memory, emotion, and cognition. Changes in the brain reliably alter conscious experience, and physical interventions such as anesthesia, brain stimulation, psychoactive drugs, injury, and neurodegenerative disease can transform or suppress awareness [@koch2016; @seth2021].

At the same time, physicalism remains philosophically controversial. Critics argue that even a complete physical description of the brain may fail to explain why subjective experience exists at all. A theory may explain neural activity, information processing, behaviour, and reportability while still leaving open the question of why these processes feel like anything from the inside [@chalmers1995; @chalmers1996].

This chapter examines physicalism as a family of theories rather than a single position. It explains why physicalism became dominant in modern consciousness research, distinguishes major forms of physicalism, evaluates the evidence supporting physicalist approaches, and considers major criticisms such as the explanatory gap, qualia, and the knowledge argument.

## Learning Objectives

After reading this chapter, the reader should be able to:

* Explain the central claim of physicalism.
* Distinguish reductive, non-reductive, functionalist, eliminative, and emergent forms of physicalism.
* Explain why physicalism became dominant in neuroscience and cognitive science.
* Describe evidence linking consciousness to physical brain processes.
* Explain the explanatory gap critique of physicalism.
* Compare physicalism with dualism, functionalism, and consciousness-first theories.
* Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of physicalist theories.
* Understand how physicalism relates to artificial intelligence and computational theories of mind.

## The Core Idea of Physicalism

Physicalism begins from the claim that consciousness is part of the natural world. Consciousness may be difficult to explain, but it is not treated as supernatural, immaterial, or outside scientific investigation. On this view, conscious experience depends on physical organization in some way.

This does not mean that all physicalists believe consciousness has already been explained. Nor does it mean that all physicalists reduce consciousness to simple neural activity. Physicalism includes a range of positions. Some physicalists argue that conscious states are identical to brain states. Others argue that consciousness emerges from complex physical systems. Others emphasize functional organization, computation, biological regulation, or information processing.

What unites these approaches is the rejection of a separate non-physical mind. Physicalists argue that a complete account of consciousness must ultimately fit within the physical world.

```{r fig-physicalism-hierarchy, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Physicalist explanatory hierarchy. Physicalist theories interpret consciousness as arising from increasingly organized physical systems ranging from fundamental physics to chemistry, biology, neural organization, and conscious experience. The highlighted transition between neural systems and subjective experience illustrates the continuing explanatory gap debated within consciousness studies.", out.width="96%", fig.align="center"}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/06_physicalism-hierarchy.png")
```

Figure @ref(fig:fig-physicalism-hierarchy) illustrates a general physicalist hierarchy. Physical systems form chemical structures, chemical structures support biological systems, biological systems include nervous systems, and sufficiently organized nervous systems may give rise to conscious experience. The most controversial transition is the final one: how neural organization becomes subjective experience.

This transition is where physicalism faces its deepest challenge. The physicalist claim is that consciousness depends on physical organization. The philosophical question is whether physical organization fully explains consciousness.

## Why Physicalism Became Dominant

Physicalism became dominant in modern consciousness research because of the strong relationship between conscious experience and physical brain processes. Consciousness changes when the brain changes. This is one of the most powerful motivations for physicalist theories.

Brain injury can alter memory, language, perception, personality, bodily awareness, attention, and selfhood. Anesthesia can suppress conscious awareness through physical intervention. Psychoactive substances can transform perception, emotion, and self-experience. Electrical stimulation of the brain can produce sensations, memories, movements, or emotional responses. Neurodegenerative diseases can progressively alter cognition, identity, and conscious functioning.

These examples strongly suggest that consciousness is deeply dependent on physical brain organization. Modern neuroscience has also made this dependence experimentally tractable through neuroimaging, electrophysiology, lesion studies, neural stimulation, anesthesia research, and computational neuroscience [@koch2016; @seth2021].

Physicalism also fits naturally with evolutionary biology. If human consciousness depends on biological systems that evolved over time, then consciousness can be investigated as part of the natural history of life rather than as a separate supernatural phenomenon. This does not solve the hard problem, but it gives physicalism a powerful scientific foundation.

For these reasons, physicalism functions as the default background assumption in much contemporary neuroscience, psychology, medicine, and cognitive science.

## Physicalism as a Response to Dualism

Physicalism is partly a response to the problems faced by dualism. Dualist theories treat consciousness as distinct from, or not fully reducible to, physical processes. Cartesian substance dualism, for example, treats mind and matter as different substances [@descartes1641].

Physicalists reject this separation. They argue that consciousness should be explained within the same natural world studied by physics, biology, neuroscience, and cognitive science. This avoids the interaction problem that challenges substance dualism: if mind is non-physical, how does it causally interact with the physical brain?

Physicalism does not deny that consciousness seems different from other physical phenomena. Rather, it argues that this difference should be explained without positing a separate non-physical realm. The goal is to understand how consciousness fits into nature.

This makes physicalism both scientifically attractive and philosophically demanding. It avoids dualist metaphysics, but it must still explain why physical processes are accompanied by subjective experience.

## Core Assumptions of Physicalism

Most physicalist theories share several broad assumptions. First, consciousness depends on physical systems. In humans and other animals, this means that conscious experience depends on the brain, nervous system, body, and biological regulation.

Second, mental states depend on physical states. Changes in the brain can change perception, memory, emotion, thought, agency, and self-experience.

Third, consciousness is part of nature. It is not treated as outside scientific explanation, even if current science does not yet explain it fully.

Fourth, consciousness can be studied empirically. Neuroscience, psychology, medicine, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence may all contribute to a physical understanding of consciousness.

Finally, physicalism rejects the need for a separate mental substance. It does not require immaterial souls, non-physical minds, or supernatural explanation.

However, physicalism is not a single unified theory. Physicalists disagree about whether consciousness can be reduced, whether it emerges, whether it is functional, whether it is computational, and whether current concepts of consciousness should be revised or eliminated.

## Major Forms of Physicalism

Physicalism includes several different approaches to the relation between mind and matter. These positions share a commitment to naturalism, but they differ in how they understand reduction, explanation, emergence, and mental properties.

### Reductive Physicalism

Reductive physicalism argues that conscious states can ultimately be reduced to physical brain states or neural mechanisms. On this view, consciousness is not merely correlated with the brain. It is identical with, or fully explainable by, physical processes.

The strongest version of this approach is identity theory. Identity theorists argue that mental states are identical to brain states [@place1956; @smart1959]. Pain, for example, would not merely be caused by neural activity; it would be a neural state described at a different level.

Reductive physicalism has the advantage of offering a clear naturalistic explanation. It treats consciousness as part of the physical world without requiring additional metaphysical principles. However, critics argue that identity theory struggles with qualia, multiple realizability, and the explanatory gap.

### Non-Reductive Physicalism

Non-reductive physicalism argues that consciousness depends entirely on physical systems but cannot be straightforwardly reduced to lower-level physical descriptions. Consciousness is physically grounded, but it may possess higher-level properties that require their own explanatory vocabulary.

This position attempts to preserve both scientific naturalism and the complexity of mental life. It accepts that consciousness depends on the physical world while resisting overly simple reductions of experience to neural activity.

Non-reductive physicalism is attractive because many sciences already use higher-level explanations. Biology is grounded in chemistry, but biological explanations are not always replaced by chemical explanations. Psychology may be grounded in neuroscience, but psychological concepts may still remain useful. The challenge is explaining how higher-level mental properties fit into the physical world without becoming either reducible or mysteriously independent [@kim2005].

### Functionalist Materialism

Functionalist forms of materialism define mental states in terms of what they do rather than what they are made of. A mental state is understood by its causal role: how it receives inputs, interacts with other states, and produces outputs [@putnam1967; @fodor1975].

Functionalism is often compatible with physicalism because functional organization must be realized in some physical system. However, it does not require that consciousness be tied to one specific biological material. In principle, different physical systems could realize the same functional organization.

This idea became highly influential in debates about artificial intelligence and machine consciousness. If consciousness depends on functional organization, then a sufficiently organized artificial system might become conscious. Critics argue, however, that functionalism may explain access, cognition, and behaviour more easily than phenomenal experience.

### Eliminative Materialism

Eliminative materialism argues that some ordinary mental concepts may eventually be replaced by more accurate scientific concepts. According to this view, folk psychological categories such as beliefs, desires, or even qualia may not correspond to real natural kinds in the way common sense assumes [@churchland1981; @churchland1986].

Eliminative materialists compare ordinary psychology to outdated scientific theories. Just as modern science abandoned concepts such as phlogiston, future neuroscience may revise or eliminate some everyday concepts of mind.

This approach is controversial because critics argue that it risks denying the very phenomenon that needs explanation. If a theory claims that qualia do not exist, it must still explain why experience appears so immediate and undeniable.

### Emergent Physicalism

Emergent physicalism proposes that consciousness emerges from sufficiently complex physical organization. Consciousness is real and physically grounded, but it may not be reducible to simple lower-level descriptions.

Emergentism is attractive because it allows consciousness to be both natural and genuinely novel. Many physical systems have higher-level properties that arise from organized complexity. Water has properties not obvious from isolated hydrogen and oxygen atoms. Living cells have properties not found in simple molecules. Similarly, consciousness may emerge from complex neural organization.

The challenge is explaining emergence clearly. If emergence means only that consciousness is complicated, then the theory may not solve the hard problem. If emergence means that consciousness has genuinely novel causal powers, then the theory must explain how those powers fit within physical causation.

## Neural Dependence of Consciousness

One of the strongest arguments for physicalism is the neural dependence of consciousness. Across many domains, conscious experience varies with brain activity.

In perception, damage to specific sensory systems can alter or eliminate conscious awareness of certain features of the world. In memory disorders, changes to the hippocampus and related structures can disrupt the continuity of experience and identity. In language disorders, brain injury can alter the ability to express or understand conscious thought. In disorders of bodily awareness, patients may lose the sense of ownership over parts of the body.

Anesthesia provides another major line of evidence. Physical changes to brain dynamics can suppress consciousness in a controlled and reversible way. Sleep and dreaming show that consciousness can be transformed even without external stimulation. Psychedelic states show that changes in neurochemistry can dramatically alter perception, selfhood, and meaning.

Split-brain research also suggests that the unity of consciousness depends on neural organization. When communication between the hemispheres is disrupted, behaviour and report can reveal surprising dissociations in awareness, action, and interpretation.

Research on disorders of consciousness, including coma, vegetative states, minimally conscious states, and locked-in syndrome, further supports the close connection between brain organization and conscious awareness [@laureys2005; @owen2006].

Together, these findings make it difficult to deny that consciousness depends deeply on physical systems. The harder question is whether dependence is the same as complete explanation.

## Correlation and Explanation

Physicalism is strongly supported by correlations between brain activity and consciousness. However, critics argue that correlation alone is not the same as explanation.

Identifying neural correlates may show when consciousness occurs, how conscious states change, and which mechanisms participate. But this may not fully explain why subjective experience exists. This concern is central to the explanatory gap [@levine1983].

The issue can be stated simply: even if every conscious state has a neural correlate, why should neural activity feel like anything from the inside? Why should physical information processing be accompanied by experience rather than occurring without awareness?

This is the central philosophical challenge for physicalism. The strongest physicalist response is that a complete neuroscience will eventually explain why the gap appears to exist. Critics respond that no amount of structural or functional description seems sufficient to derive subjective experience.

## Physicalism and the Hard Problem

Physicalist theories differ in how they approach the hard problem. Some physicalists accept the hard problem as a genuine challenge but argue that it will eventually be solved by neuroscience, cognitive science, or a more mature theory of mind. Others argue that the hard problem is based on misleading intuitions about experience [@dennett1991; @frankish2016].

Reductionist physicalists often argue that consciousness will be identified with physical mechanisms. Functionalists argue that consciousness can be explained by causal organization and information processing. Higher-order and representational approaches argue that conscious experience depends on how mental states are represented or made available to cognition. Illusionists argue that phenomenal consciousness, as traditionally conceived, may be a cognitive illusion [@frankish2016].

Critics of physicalism argue that these responses still fail to explain why physical processes are accompanied by subjective feeling. Chalmers’ hard problem and Jackson’s knowledge argument both challenge the idea that physical explanation is sufficient [@jackson1982; @chalmers1995; @chalmers1996].

Physicalism therefore faces a central question: can subjective experience be fully explained in physical terms, or does consciousness reveal a limitation in physical explanation?

## Physicalism, Qualia, and the Knowledge Argument

Qualia are the qualitative features of experience, such as the redness of red, the painfulness of pain, or the taste of bitterness. Physicalists must explain how such qualitative features fit into the physical world.

One of the most influential challenges is Frank Jackson’s Mary’s Room thought experiment. Mary is a scientist who knows all the physical facts about colour vision but has lived in a black-and-white environment. When she sees red for the first time, does she learn something new? If she does, then complete physical knowledge may not include all knowledge about conscious experience [@jackson1982].

Physicalists have responded in several ways. Some argue that Mary gains a new ability rather than new factual knowledge. Others argue that she gains acquaintance with an experience she already knew about physically. Still others argue that the thought experiment depends on an unrealistic idea of complete physical knowledge.

The knowledge argument remains important because it captures a persistent worry about physicalism: objective physical description may leave out the subjective character of experience.

## Multiple Realizability and Physicalism

Another challenge for reductive physicalism is multiple realizability. If the same mental state can be realized by different physical systems, then mental states may not be identical to specific neural states.

For example, pain in humans, animals, or possible artificial systems might be implemented by different physical mechanisms while playing similar functional roles. This idea was central to functionalist criticisms of strict identity theory [@putnam1967; @fodor1975].

Multiple realizability does not refute all forms of physicalism. A physicalist can argue that every mental state must be physically realized, even if it is not always realized in the same physical way. However, it challenges simple reductions of mental states to particular human brain states.

This is one reason contemporary physicalism often takes non-reductive, functionalist, or emergent forms rather than strict identity theory.

## Physicalism and Artificial Intelligence

Physicalism has important implications for artificial intelligence. If consciousness depends on physical organization, then the question becomes: what kind of physical organization is sufficient?

Functionalist and computational physicalists are more open to the possibility of machine consciousness. If consciousness depends on causal structure, information processing, global availability, or self-modeling, then artificial systems might become conscious if they instantiate the relevant organization [@dehaene2014; @butlin2023].

Other physicalists are more cautious. Biological and embodied approaches argue that consciousness may depend on living systems, bodily regulation, affect, homeostasis, and organism-environment interaction [@varela1991; @thompson2007; @seth2021]. From this perspective, current artificial systems may simulate intelligent behaviour without having subjective experience.

This debate shows that physicalism does not automatically imply that AI systems can be conscious. It depends on what kind of physical, biological, functional, or computational organization a theory considers necessary.

## Strengths of Physicalism

Physicalism has several major strengths. First, it is highly compatible with science. It fits naturally with neuroscience, biology, medicine, psychology, and empirical investigation.

Second, physicalism generates productive research programs. The search for neural correlates of consciousness, studies of anesthesia, research on perception and attention, computational neuroscience, and investigations of disorders of consciousness all depend on physicalist assumptions [@crick1994; @koch2016; @dehaene2011; @seth2021].

Third, physicalism integrates consciousness with evolutionary biology. Consciousness can be studied as a biological phenomenon that developed through natural processes rather than as a separate immaterial entity.

Fourth, physicalism avoids the interaction problem that challenges dualism. If consciousness is physical or physically realized, then there is no need to explain how a non-physical mind affects a physical brain.

Finally, physicalism connects consciousness research with broader scientific accounts of matter, life, computation, information, and biological organization.

## Weaknesses and Criticisms

Despite its strengths, physicalism faces serious criticisms. The most important is the explanatory gap. Critics argue that physical explanations may describe neural dynamics, behaviour, cognition, and information processing without explaining subjective feeling itself [@levine1983].

The knowledge argument raises a related challenge by suggesting that complete physical knowledge may still fail to capture what experience is like [@jackson1982]. Qualia critiques argue that the qualitative features of experience resist purely structural, computational, or functional description.

Physicalism also faces challenges concerning intentionality, meaning, selfhood, and lived experience. A physical system may process information, but it remains difficult to explain how information becomes meaningful for a subject.

Finally, some critics argue that physicalism may be too broad. If everything must ultimately be physical, then the central question becomes what kind of physical explanation is needed. Without a specific theory, physicalism can become a general worldview rather than a detailed account of consciousness.

## Physicalism and Other Theories

Physicalism differs from dualism by rejecting a separate non-physical mind. It differs from panpsychism by usually denying that consciousness is fundamental or widespread throughout nature. It differs from consciousness-first theories by treating consciousness as dependent on physical organization rather than as the foundation of reality.

However, physicalism overlaps with several major theories discussed later in this book. Global Workspace Theory is often physicalist because it explains consciousness through neural broadcasting and cognitive access [@baars1988; @dehaene2011]. Integrated Information Theory is more complex: it is naturalistic and formal, but it also treats consciousness as intrinsic to certain causal structures [@tononi2004; @oizumi2014]. Predictive Processing and the Bayesian brain framework are usually physicalist because they explain perception and cognition through embodied prediction, inference, and neural dynamics [@friston2010; @clark2013].

Physicalism is therefore not one theory among many in a simple way. It is a broad metaphysical and scientific background within which many specific theories operate.

## Evaluation

Physicalism remains the dominant framework in scientific consciousness research because it aligns strongly with neuroscience, biology, medicine, computation, and empirical methodology. It explains why changes in the brain alter conscious experience and provides a powerful basis for experimental research.

However, physicalism remains philosophically contested. The central unresolved issue is whether physical explanation can fully account for phenomenal experience. A physicalist theory may explain neural mechanisms, functional organization, and behavioural capacities, but critics argue that this may still leave unanswered why experience exists at all.

For this reason, physicalism is both powerful and incomplete. It is powerful because consciousness clearly depends on physical systems in humans and other animals. It is incomplete because the precise relation between physical organization and subjective experience remains unresolved.

The future of physicalism depends on whether neuroscience, cognitive science, computational theory, and philosophy can together explain not only the mechanisms associated with consciousness, but also the first-person character of experience itself.

## Chapter Summary

Physicalism is the view that consciousness is ultimately part of the physical world. It rejects separate mental substances and attempts to explain consciousness through neural, biological, computational, functional, or emergent physical organization.

Major forms of physicalism include reductive physicalism, identity theory, non-reductive physicalism, functionalist materialism, eliminative materialism, and emergent physicalism. These positions differ in how they understand reduction, emergence, and explanation.

Physicalism is strongly supported by the dependence of consciousness on brain activity. Brain injury, anesthesia, psychoactive substances, sleep, dreaming, neural stimulation, and disorders of consciousness all show that changes in physical systems can alter conscious experience.

The major challenge for physicalism is the explanatory gap. Critics argue that physical descriptions may explain mechanisms and functions without explaining why experience feels like anything from the inside. The knowledge argument, qualia, multiple realizability, and questions of meaning and subjectivity all continue to challenge physicalist theories.

Physicalism remains the dominant scientific framework for consciousness research, but whether it can fully explain subjective experience remains one of the central unresolved questions in the field.

<!--chapter:end:06-materialism-physicalism.Rmd-->

# Functionalism {#functionalism}

## Chapter Overview

Functionalism is one of the most influential approaches in contemporary philosophy of mind, cognitive science, artificial intelligence, and consciousness research. Rather than defining mental states by what they are physically made of, functionalism defines them by what they do. A mental state is understood in terms of its causal role within a larger system: how it receives input, interacts with other internal states, guides behaviour, and contributes to cognition.

Pain, for example, is not defined primarily as a particular biological substance or neural structure. Instead, it is understood by its functional role: it is typically caused by bodily damage, produces unpleasant experience, motivates avoidance or protection, influences memory and learning, and interacts with beliefs, desires, attention, and action. On this view, what makes pain pain is not simply its material composition, but its place within an organized system of causal relations.

Functionalism transformed the study of mind by shifting attention away from strict biological identity and toward causal organization, information processing, computation, and cognitive architecture. This shift became foundational for cognitive science, artificial intelligence, computational neuroscience, Global Workspace Theory, predictive processing, higher-order theories, and many contemporary models of conscious access [@putnam1967; @fodor1968; @baars1988; @dehaene2011].

At the same time, functionalism remains controversial. Critics argue that functional organization may explain cognition, behaviour, reportability, and intelligent processing without fully explaining subjective experience. A system might perform the right functions, process information in the right way, and behave intelligently, yet it remains unclear whether there is something it is like to be that system. For this reason, functionalism lies at the center of debates about artificial intelligence, machine consciousness, qualia, and the hard problem of consciousness [@block1978; @searle1980; @chalmers1996].

## Learning Objectives

After reading this chapter, the reader should be able to:

* Define the central claim of functionalism.
* Explain how functionalism differs from behaviourism and identity theory.
* Describe the principle of multiple realizability.
* Distinguish major forms of functionalism.
* Explain why functionalism became influential in cognitive science and artificial intelligence.
* Evaluate functionalism’s strengths and limitations.
* Explain functionalism’s relationship to access consciousness and phenomenal consciousness.
* Analyze criticisms concerning qualia, subjective experience, and machine consciousness.

## The Core Idea of Functionalism

The central claim of functionalism is that mental states are individuated by their causal-functional roles rather than by their physical substance. A mental state is what it does within a system.

This idea can be understood by comparison with ordinary functional objects. A clock is a clock because it performs the function of keeping time. It may be made of gears, circuits, software, or atomic oscillations. The material matters for implementation, but the identity of the clock depends on the role it plays. Similarly, functionalists argue that mental states may be identified by their role in cognition rather than by a single biological material.

Applied to consciousness, functionalism asks what role conscious states play in perception, memory, attention, reasoning, self-monitoring, and action. It shifts the central question from “What material is consciousness made of?” to “What causal organization makes a state mental or conscious?”

This shift allowed mental states to be studied scientifically without reducing them immediately to specific neural states. It also opened the possibility that different physical systems could realize similar mental functions.

## Why Functionalism Was Revolutionary

Functionalism was revolutionary because it offered a third path between behaviourism and identity theory.

Behaviourism attempted to define mental states in terms of observable behaviour. It emphasized experimental rigor, prediction, and measurable response, but it often neglected internal cognitive organization [@watson1913; @skinner1953]. Identity theory, by contrast, identified mental states directly with brain states [@place1956; @smart1959]. This made mind fully physical, but it risked tying mental states too closely to specific biological structures.

Functionalism avoided both extremes. Unlike behaviourism, it accepted internal mental states and causal organization. Unlike strict identity theory, it did not require that a mental state be identical to one specific neural state. What mattered was the role a state played within a system.

This approach became highly influential because it fit naturally with the rise of cognitive science. The mind could be studied as an organized information-processing system. Mental states could be analyzed in terms of inputs, internal transitions, representations, memory, attention, decision-making, and outputs. This made functionalism especially important for artificial intelligence and computational theories of mind [@putnam1967; @fodor1968; @lewis1972].

## Historical Development

Functionalism emerged in the mid-twentieth century as philosophers and cognitive scientists reconsidered how mental states should be explained. Earlier behaviourist approaches had tried to avoid inner mental life by focusing on observable behaviour. However, language, reasoning, planning, memory, and flexible problem-solving seemed to require internal structure.

At the same time, strict identity theory appeared too narrow. If pain is identical to a particular human brain state, then creatures with different nervous systems might not be able to feel pain. Functionalists argued that this was implausible. A dog, octopus, alien, or artificial system might have a different physical structure while still possessing a state that plays the functional role of pain.

Hilary Putnam’s arguments for multiple realizability were especially influential [@putnam1967]. Jerry Fodor developed functionalist ideas within cognitive science and the computational theory of mind [@fodor1968]. David Lewis and David Armstrong contributed analytic and causal-role versions of functionalism [@lewis1972; @armstrong1968]. Later philosophers such as Sydney Shoemaker and Ned Block developed important refinements and criticisms [@shoemaker1981; @block1978].

Functionalism therefore became both a theory of mind and a bridge between philosophy, psychology, computation, and neuroscience.

## Functional Organization

Functionalism interprets mental life as an organized network of causal relations. Sensory inputs affect internal states. Internal states interact with memory, attention, belief, emotion, and reasoning. These interactions guide behaviour, speech, learning, planning, and self-monitoring.

```{r fig-functionalist-view, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Functionalist models define mental states according to causal organization, information flow, internal processing, and behavioural relations rather than specific physical substance. The figure also illustrates multiple realizability and contrasts functionalism with identity theory.", out.width="97%", fig.align="center"} id="84951h"
knitr::include_graphics("figures/07_functionalist_view.png")
```

Figure @ref(fig:fig-functionalist-view) illustrates the basic functionalist framework. Mental states are defined not by a single physical material, but by their place within a larger system of input, internal processing, and output. The same functional organization could, in principle, be realized by different physical systems.

This idea is one of functionalism’s most important contributions. It makes mental explanation more flexible than identity theory while remaining compatible with physicalism. Mental states must be realized in some physical system, but they are not necessarily identical with one specific physical structure.

However, the same figure also points toward functionalism’s central problem. Even if a system has the right functional organization, does that guarantee subjective experience? Or does functionalism explain only the structure of cognition and behaviour?

## Multiple Realizability

Multiple realizability is one of the strongest arguments for functionalism. It is the idea that the same mental state can be realized in different physical systems, provided that the relevant causal-functional organization is preserved.

Pain provides a common example. Human pain, animal pain, and possible alien pain might be implemented by different biological mechanisms. Yet if each state is caused by damage, produces distress, motivates protection, influences learning, and interacts with other cognitive states in the right way, then functionalists argue that each could count as pain.

This argument challenges strict identity theory. If mental states can be realized in different physical systems, then they cannot simply be identical to one specific human neural state. Instead, mental states must be understood at a more abstract functional level [@putnam1967; @fodor1968].

Multiple realizability also became central to artificial intelligence. If mental states depend on organization rather than biological material, then artificial systems might possess mental states if they instantiate the right functional structure. This possibility remains one of the main reasons functionalism continues to matter for debates about machine consciousness.

## Major Forms of Functionalism

Functionalism is not a single unified theory. It is a broad family of approaches that define mental states by role, organization, and causal structure. Different versions disagree about how these roles should be specified.

### Machine-State Functionalism

Machine-state functionalism compares the mind to a computational system. A system has inputs, internal states, transition rules, and outputs. Mental states are understood as states within this organized system.

This version was strongly influenced by computation and early artificial intelligence. It made it possible to think of the mind as a kind of information-processing architecture. The appeal of this model is its clarity: mental states can be described formally in terms of causal transitions.

However, critics argue that machine-state functionalism can become too abstract. A formal description of state transitions may not capture embodiment, emotion, biological regulation, or subjective experience.

### Psycho-Functionalism

Psycho-functionalism defines mental states using the best available scientific psychology rather than ordinary language. Instead of asking how common sense describes pain, belief, or desire, psycho-functionalism asks what roles these states play in mature cognitive science.

This version is attractive because it connects functionalism with empirical research. Mental states are not analyzed only through folk psychology but through attention, memory, perception, learning, reasoning, and cognitive architecture.

Psycho-functionalism is especially important for cognitive neuroscience because it allows mental states to be studied as functional components of larger cognitive systems.

### Analytic Functionalism

Analytic functionalism attempts to analyze mental concepts through their ordinary causal roles. For example, pain may be analyzed as the state typically caused by injury, associated with distress, and likely to produce avoidance behaviour.

This approach is closely connected to conceptual analysis. It asks what our ordinary mental concepts mean and how they relate to other concepts. Its strength is philosophical clarity. Its weakness is that ordinary language may not accurately reflect the underlying nature of mind.

### Computational Functionalism

Computational functionalism treats mental states as computational processes implemented in physical systems. It is closely related to the computational theory of mind and artificial intelligence [@fodor1968; @turing1950].

On this view, cognition involves information processing, representation, symbolic or sub-symbolic computation, and transformations among internal states. Consciousness may then be understood in terms of computational architecture, information availability, self-modeling, or global access.

Computational functionalism has strongly influenced AI and cognitive science. However, critics argue that computation alone may not be sufficient for understanding or consciousness. This criticism is central to Searle’s Chinese Room argument [@searle1980].

### Teleofunctionalism

Teleofunctionalism explains mental states partly through their biological or evolutionary functions. A mental state is understood by the role it was selected or developed to perform within an organism.

This approach connects functionalism with biology. It is especially useful for explaining perception, emotion, pain, and adaptive behaviour. However, it may be less straightforward when applied to artificial systems, since machines may not have evolutionary histories in the same sense as organisms.

## Functionalism and Consciousness

Functionalism is especially powerful for explaining access consciousness. Access consciousness concerns information availability for reasoning, report, memory, decision-making, and action [@block1995]. Functionalism naturally explains how information can become available to a system and influence behaviour.

For example, a functionalist account can explain how a visual stimulus is processed, selected by attention, held in working memory, compared with prior knowledge, reported verbally, and used to guide action. This makes functionalism highly compatible with theories such as Global Workspace Theory, which explains consciousness in terms of global availability or broadcasting of information [@baars1988; @dehaene2011].

However, functionalism is more controversial when applied to phenomenal consciousness. Phenomenal consciousness concerns subjective experience itself: what it is like to see red, feel pain, hear music, or experience oneself as a subject. Critics argue that functionalism may explain what consciousness does without explaining why consciousness feels like anything from the inside [@chalmers1995; @chalmers1996].

This distinction is central. Functionalism gives powerful accounts of cognition, reportability, attention, and intelligent behaviour. Its unresolved challenge is whether those accounts fully explain subjective experience.

## Functionalism and Artificial Intelligence

Functionalism is one of the most important philosophical foundations of artificial intelligence. If mental states are defined by causal organization rather than biological material, then artificial systems might possess mental states if they have the right functional structure.

This idea supports the possibility of machine consciousness. A sufficiently advanced artificial system might integrate information, monitor its internal states, use memory, form goals, respond flexibly, and report its own condition. From a functionalist perspective, these capacities may be relevant to consciousness.

However, functionalism also raises a difficult question: does functional simulation instantiate consciousness, or does it only imitate conscious behaviour? A chatbot, robot, or artificial neural network may produce intelligent outputs, but it remains unclear whether there is anything it is like to be that system.

This issue has become more important with recent debates about AI consciousness. Some researchers argue that machine consciousness should be evaluated using theory-based indicators, including global availability, self-modeling, attention, recurrent processing, agency, and embodiment [@butlin2023]. Others caution that intelligent behaviour and language generation should not be confused with subjective experience.

Functionalism therefore makes AI consciousness possible in principle, but it does not settle whether any current artificial system is conscious.

## Functionalism and Modern Consciousness Theories

Many contemporary theories of consciousness contain functionalist elements. Global Workspace Theory explains consciousness through the functional role of broadcasting information across cognitive systems [@baars1988; @dehaene2011]. Higher-Order theories explain consciousness through the representation or monitoring of mental states [@rosenthal2005; @lau2011]. Attention Schema Theory explains consciousness through the brain’s functional model of attention [@graziano2013].

Predictive Processing and the Bayesian brain framework also have functionalist dimensions. They explain perception and cognition in terms of prediction, error correction, and hierarchical inference [@friston2010; @clark2013]. These accounts focus on what cognitive systems do: predict sensory input, update internal models, regulate action, and reduce uncertainty.

Functionalism therefore remains deeply embedded in contemporary consciousness science. Even theories that are not purely functionalist often rely on functional concepts such as information access, monitoring, control, integration, representation, and reportability.

At the same time, theories differ in whether they treat these functions as sufficient for consciousness or merely as correlates and mechanisms associated with consciousness.

## Embodiment and Enactive Challenges

Embodied and enactive theorists criticize overly abstract forms of functionalism. They argue that cognition and consciousness cannot be fully understood as internal information processing alone. Instead, mind depends on bodily action, affect, sensorimotor engagement, biological regulation, and interaction with the environment [@varela1991; @thompson2007].

From this perspective, a purely functional description may leave out the lived, embodied character of experience. Consciousness is not merely information moving through an abstract system. It is the experience of an organism situated in a world.

This critique is especially important for artificial intelligence. A system may have sophisticated computational functions while lacking bodily needs, affective regulation, vulnerability, homeostasis, or sensorimotor engagement. Embodied theorists therefore question whether abstract computation alone is sufficient for consciousness.

Functionalists can respond that embodiment itself can be described functionally. If bodily regulation and environmental interaction are necessary, then they can be included in the functional organization. The debate then becomes whether functionalism can expand enough to include embodiment, or whether embodiment reveals limits in the functionalist framework.

## Classic Criticisms of Functionalism

Functionalism has faced several influential philosophical criticisms. Most of them focus on the possibility that functional organization may not be sufficient for subjective experience.

### Absent Qualia

The absent qualia objection argues that a system might have the correct functional organization while lacking conscious experience entirely. Such a system would process information, produce behaviour, and interact with its environment in the right way, but there would be nothing it is like to be that system.
